bottleneck: Epigenetic editors (dCas9 fused to methyltransferases or activators) can switch genes on or off without changing DNA, but the marks fade: cell division and endogenous epigenetic machinery gradually erase engineered methylation and histone modifications. Durability beyond weeks to months in vivo is unproven, and off-target epigenetic changes may alter neighboring genes unpredictably, with effects that are harder to detect than DNA edits. The reversibility that makes the approach attractive also makes it transient.
current_state: Epigenetic editing works in cell models and short animal studies. No therapy has yet demonstrated durable, heritable epigenetic correction in patients.

title: Epigenetic edits fade as cells divide
why_it_blocks: Reversible, DNA-sparing gene control would be safer than permanent edits — if it lasted. Without durability, epigenetic editing is a transient drug with a gene-therapy price tag, failing on both safety and economics.
